findings.documented: The API key is supplied as the api_key query parameter, and protected requests use the documented token.
findings.actual: The live API requires the key in an X-API-Key request header. Sending it as a query parameter returns 401 with the message 'send your key in the X-API-Key request header, not as a query parameter'.
findings.how_found: Sent the key using the documented query parameter, got a 401 whose detail message named the correct header, then confirmed X-API-Key works.
findings.impact: Clients following the documented authentication flow cannot authenticate at all.

findings.documented: Login returns token and expires_in: 86400, with a full demo-user object.
findings.actual: Login returns access_token, refresh_token, refresh_url, token_type Bearer, expires_in 900 (15 minutes), and a user object containing only the email.
findings.how_found: Called the login endpoint and inspected the response body and its keys directly.
findings.impact: A frontend relying on the documented field names or a 24-hour token lifetime will fail to authenticate or will silently drop the session after 15 minutes.

findings.documented: There is no refresh flow; a single login is enough for one working session.
findings.actual: POST /auth/refresh accepts {"refresh_token": ...} and returns a fresh access_token/refresh_token pair with the same shape as login.
findings.how_found: Called the refresh_url returned by login with the refresh token and confirmed a new access token was issued.
findings.impact: Without using this endpoint, a session would be forced to log in again every 15 minutes instead of refreshing silently.

findings.documented: Logout invalidates the current token server side.
findings.actual: Logout returns {"ok": true, "note": "tokens are stateless; discard them client side"}. The same access token still works on a protected request made immediately after logout.
findings.how_found: Called logout, then reused the same access token for GET /v1/saved and got a normal 200 response instead of 401.
findings.impact: A frontend must discard tokens client-side on logout; the server performs no revocation, so a leaked token remains valid until it expires.

findings.documented: Collections use page and limit, with a maximum limit of 200.
findings.actual: Collections use offset and limit. A requested limit of 200 (or any value above 50) is silently capped to 50, and responses include count, total, has_more, results, limit, and offset instead of page/page_size.
findings.how_found: Requested /v1/listings, /v1/rentals, and /v1/projects with limit values of 1, 10, 50, 100, 200, 500, and 1000 and compared the returned record counts.
findings.impact: Clients must page with offset += count while has_more is true; requesting page and a limit above 50 will silently under-fetch.

findings.documented: total is the exact number of records matching your filters; divide it by limit to compute all pages.
findings.actual: total stays fixed at a stale value (e.g. 3841 for unfiltered /v1/listings) at every offset, while paging to has_more:false actually returns 4100 listings, 1550 rentals, and 460 projects -- 6-7% more records than total reports in every case checked, including under the locality filter (total=414, actual=442).
findings.how_found: Requested /v1/listings, /v1/rentals, and /v1/projects at increasing offsets up to and past the point where has_more became false, and recorded total at each offset alongside the actual record count returned.
findings.impact: Clients cannot compute the last page from total; they must traverse with has_more to reach the true end of a collection, or they will silently miss the last ~6-7% of records.

findings.documented: Returns active sale listings; inactive, expired and withdrawn listings are excluded server side.
findings.actual: The endpoint returns both is_live:true and is_live:false records (867 of the 4100 retrievable records are is_live:false); the client must filter on is_live itself.
findings.how_found: Downloaded every retrievable listing record and tallied the is_live field.
findings.impact: A frontend that shows every returned listing without checking is_live will display withdrawn/inactive properties as available.

findings.documented: furnishing, is_live, and project_id are documented query parameters; min_price and max_price are documented as inclusive rupee filters.
findings.actual: All five parameters are accepted (no error) but ignored: requests with furnishing=fully-furnished, is_live=false, project_id=<id>, or min_price/max_price set all returned the exact same records, in the same order, as an unfiltered request -- including records priced outside the requested min_price/max_price range.
findings.how_found: Ran matched pairs of filtered vs. unfiltered requests against /v1/listings and compared the actual field values of every returned record.
findings.impact: A frontend must apply furnishing, is_live, project_id, min_price, and max_price filtering locally after fetching, not rely on the server to filter.

findings.documented: A listing detail is available at the singular /v1/listing/{listing_id} path.
findings.actual: The singular path returns 404 ("Not Found") for a real listing_id.
findings.how_found: Requested the documented route with a real listing ID obtained from /v1/listings.
findings.impact: Clients must use the plural detail route instead.

findings.documented: No plural listing detail route is documented.
findings.actual: GET /v1/listings/{listing_id} returns the full listing detail object for a real listing_id.
findings.how_found: Retried the same listing ID against the plural collection path after the singular path 404'd.
findings.impact: This is the working route the frontend uses for listing detail pages.

findings.documented: Returns up to ten comparable listings (same locality, same bedroom count, price within 15%).
findings.actual: The route returns 404 ("Not Found") for a real listing_id.
findings.how_found: Requested the documented similar-listings route with a real listing ID.
findings.impact: A "you may also like" component must be derived client-side from the bulk-downloaded dataset instead of calling this endpoint.

findings.documented: Saved listings use GET, POST { "id": ... }, and DELETE /v1/favourites/{id}.
findings.actual: GET and POST /v1/favourites both return 404 ("Not Found").
findings.how_found: Called GET and POST /v1/favourites exactly as documented.
findings.impact: Clients must use the live /v1/saved routes instead of /v1/favourites.

findings.documented: No /v1/saved route is documented.
findings.actual: GET /v1/saved lists a user's saved listings ({"count": ..., "results": [...]}), and POST /v1/saved with body {"listing_id": "..."} saves one (POSTing the documented {"id": ...} body instead returns 422, "Field required: listing_id").
findings.how_found: Tested list and save operations with a real listing_id against several undocumented candidate paths, then removed the test save with DELETE.
findings.impact: This is the working saved-listing API the frontend must implement against.

findings.documented: No live delete route is documented under /v1/saved.
findings.actual: DELETE /v1/saved/{listing_id} removes a saved listing and returns {"ok": true, "listing_id": ..., "saved_count": ...}.
findings.how_found: Completed the save -> list -> delete lifecycle end-to-end with one real listing.
findings.impact: The frontend can implement persistent per-user saved listings using this route.

findings.documented: Returns pre-computed aggregates for the candidate's city (total_listings, median_price, median_price_per_sqft, by_locality, by_bhk).
findings.actual: The route returns 404 ("Not Found") both before and after authenticating.
findings.how_found: Requested the documented analytics route with a valid API key and a valid bearer token.
findings.impact: The insights screen must compute every aggregate itself from the bulk-downloaded /v1/listings, /v1/rentals, and /v1/projects collections; there is no server-side summary to fall back on.

findings.documented: price_min and price_max are in rupees, everywhere in the API.
findings.actual: price_min and price_max are each independently encoded as either lakhs or crores of rupees, not rupees: every raw value across all 460 projects falls into one of two disjoint bands (roughly 1.0-3.78 or 70.2-99.9) with nothing in between. Values under 10 are already in crores (multiply by 1e7); values 10 and over are in lakhs (multiply by 1e5). Reading both fields as the same unit produces 357 projects where price_min > price_max, which is impossible; applying the per-field split leaves zero such violations. The live API's own sort_by=price_max ordering independently confirms this exact conversion (a raw value of 70.2 sorts as smaller than a raw value of 1.01, i.e. the server itself treats 70.2 as 0.702 crore).
findings.how_found: Sorted every project's raw price_min and price_max, found the two-band gap, verified the per-field conversion eliminates all min>max violations (versus 357 under a naive same-unit reading), then cross-checked it against the live sort_by=price_max endpoint parameter.
findings.impact: Displaying price_min/price_max as raw rupees, or converting them with a single shared rule instead of per-field, makes every project's price wrong and changes which project is reported as costliest.

findings.documented: Area fields are in square feet, integer, everywhere in the API.
findings.actual: About 337 of 842 magichomes-sourced listings (the listing_id prefix MAG-) report carpet_area and super_built_up_area in square metres instead of square feet. Every other source website (100acres, dwelling, squarelane, zerobroker) is consistently in square feet for every bedroom count; the affected magichomes records are 5-10x smaller than the smallest legitimate square-foot value for the same bedroom count, with a large, clean gap and nothing in between. Multiplying the affected values by 10.7639 (sqm->sqft) restores them to the normal range while preserving the same ~1.33x super_built_up_area/carpet_area ratio seen everywhere else, and resolves several near-duplicate listing pairs whose areas otherwise looked ~90% different.
findings.how_found: Computed the minimum carpet_area per bedroom count from the four non-magichomes source websites, then found magichomes records far below that floor; verified the super_built_up/carpet_area ratio and cross-checked against magichomes duplicates on other source sites (e.g. MAG-4003717 carpet_area 69 vs. its ZER-4003843 duplicate's carpet_area 736; 69 sqm = 743 sqft).
findings.impact: Any price-per-square-foot calculation (including this submission's avg_price_per_sqft_2bhk) is roughly 40% too high if magichomes areas are used as-is; areas and price/sqft must be corrected for these records before display or calculation.

findings.documented: Timestamps are ISO 8601, UTC, with a Z suffix, everywhere in the API.
findings.actual: Every one of the 4100 retrievable /v1/listings posted_at values is timezone-naive (no Z, no offset, e.g. 2026-01-19T12:56:00), while every one of the 1550 retrievable /v1/rentals posted_at values carries a Z suffix (e.g. 2026-06-02T03:58:00Z). The convention is not applied uniformly across endpoints.
findings.how_found: Checked the trailing characters of posted_at on every downloaded listing and rental record; 4100/4100 listings are naive and 1550/1550 rentals end in Z.
findings.impact: Date-based calculations (e.g. counting listings posted in a window before REFERENCE) must interpret naive /v1/listings timestamps explicitly as Asia/Kolkata (matching /health's own timezone) rather than assuming UTC.

findings.documented: total_listings is recomputed whenever a listing is added or withdrawn, so it always agrees with GET /v1/listings?project_id=....
findings.actual: 119 of 460 projects have a total_listings value that disagrees with the number of retrievable is_live:true listings that reference that project_id (336 disagree if inactive listings are counted too); 57 projects report total_listings:0 while 52 of those actually have one or more live listings linked to them.
findings.how_found: Grouped all retrievable listings by project_id and is_live, then compared each project's reported total_listings against both the live-only and all-record counts.
findings.impact: total_listings cannot be trusted for display or for the projects_with_wrong_listing_count calculation; the real count must be derived by filtering /v1/listings by project_id and is_live client-side.

findings.documented: Listing records describe ordinary real properties.
findings.actual: 45 records contain structurally impossible values, in five disjoint groups of exactly nine each: negative price, floor greater than the building's own total_floors (by 3-14 floors), bedroom:0 on a non-plot property (with carpet areas up to 1962 sqft, i.e. not studios), super_built_up_area smaller than carpet_area (impossible, since super built-up must include the carpet area), and latitude/longitude swapped or otherwise outside the rest of the dataset's Chennai-area bounds.
findings.how_found: Tested five independent structural invariants across the complete listing download and confirmed each violating group is clean (a large gap between violating and legitimate values, e.g. floor exceeds total_floors by at least 3 with zero near-miss cases).
findings.impact: These records if displayed would mislead users; they are excluded from this submission's avg_price_per_sqft_2bhk calculation and reported as corrupt_listing_ids.

findings.documented: Listing records are genuine property listings.
findings.actual: 9 records advertise full-property sales at implausible prices between 6,470 and 16,320 rupees -- less than a single month's rent for a comparable unit, and a 72x jump below the next-cheapest genuine listing (1,160,000) with a clean gap and nothing in between. These are bait listings meant to generate enquiries, not genuine sale prices.
findings.how_found: Sorted every positive listing price and found a cluster of exactly 9 records far below the rest of the distribution, then reviewed each one's full record for internal plausibility (normal bedroom counts, normal areas, verified=true on most) confirming they are not simply corrupt/impossible records.
findings.impact: These records are excluded from the avg_price_per_sqft_2bhk calculation and reported as fake_listing_ids; a frontend should flag or hide them rather than surface them as real deals.

findings.documented: "posted_at" is a sort_by option and the API respects this parameter.
findings.actual: There is no consistent sorting based on "posted_at".
findings.how_found: Requested /v1/listings?sort_by=posted_at&limit=50&offset=0&order=asc with sort_by=posted_at and inspected the returned records' posted_at values; they were not in chronological order. For example, SQU-4003146 (posted_at 2026-01-13T20:39:00) appears before ZER-4002522 (posted_at 2026-01-13T17:34:00).
findings.impact: The frontend cannot rely on the server to sort by posted_at; it must sort locally after fetching.

findings.documented: "carpet_area" is a sort_by option and the API respects this parameter.
findings.actual: Some malformed records have carpet_area values that are 10x smaller than the rest of the dataset (see units finding above), and these records sort as if they are the smallest carpet_area in the dataset, even though they are actually larger when converted to square feet.
findings.how_found: Requested /v1/listings?sort_by=carpet_area&limit=50&offset=0&order=asc with sort_by=carpet_area and inspected the returned records' carpet_area values; they were not in the expected order. For example, 100-4003374 (carpet_area 366) appears before MAG-4002620 (carpet_area 34). BUT BUT here's the catch, 34 square meters is roughly equal to 366 square feet. If we consider that correction, then the sorting works.
findings.impact: The frontend cannot rely on the server to sort by carpet_area; it must convert the values to the same unit and sort locally after fetching.

findings.documented: "price_max" and "price_min" are sort_by options and the API respects these parameters.
findings.actual: The price_max and price_min fields are encoded in two different units (lakhs and crores) depending on the value, and the server does not normalize them when sorting. As a result, projects with price_max in lakhs will appear to be cheaper than those in crores, even though they are actually more expensive when converted to the same unit.
findings.how_found: Requested /v1/projects?sort_by=price_max&limit=50&offset=0&order=asc with sort_by=price_max and inspected the returned records' price_max values; they were not in the expected order. For example, P40231 (price_max 99.8) appears before P40160 (price_max 1.01) and P40381 (price_min 99.9) appears before P40010 (price_min 1.01). But again, if we consider correct units, 1.01 crore is more than 99.9 lakhs. So the sorting is correct after conversion.
findings.impact: The frontend cannot rely on the server to sort by price_max; it must convert the values to the same unit and sort locally after fetching.
